Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- 54-year-old male with untreated hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, and smoking history presents with 2-hour mid-sternal pressure (7/10) radiating to left shoulder/arm, plus dyspnoea, light-headedness, nausea. Also reports recent exertional dyspnoea, calf pain, and leg swelling.  
- Differential diagnoses (consistent with transcript and DDx):  
  • Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) – high likelihood given classic pressure-type pain, radiation, autonomic symptoms, and multiple cardiovascular risk factors.  
  • Pulmonary embolism – moderate likelihood due to acute dyspnoea and history of calf pain/leg swelling (possible DVT).  
  • Aortic dissection – lower likelihood but considered because of long-standing hypertension and abrupt chest pain.  
- Immediate plan: clinician advised patient to call emergency services; ambulance dispatched; patient instructed to remain calm, avoid medications, and await paramedics. Information to be relayed to emergency team on arrival.  

Management Plan
- Emergency transfer to hospital via ambulance for ECG, cardiac enzymes, chest imaging, and further management of suspected ACS/PE.  
- Initiate guideline-based ACS protocol in ED if confirmed (e.g., antiplatelets, anticoagulation, nitrates as appropriate).  
- Smoking cessation counselling once acute issue stabilised.  
- Long-term management of hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia to be addressed post-discharge.  
- Follow-up telehealth appointment arranged after hospital evaluation.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Acute coronary syndrome (unstable angina/NSTEMI) – High likelihood: typical chest pressure with left-arm radiation, risk factors, autonomic symptoms.  
2. Pulmonary embolism – Moderate likelihood: acute dyspnoea, chest discomfort, calf pain/leg swelling suggesting possible DVT.  
3. Aortic dissection – Low–moderate likelihood: abrupt chest pain in setting of uncontrolled hypertension, though pain quality less typical.
